I'm working through the geometry of each stored part, starting with the base plate's bounding box and the pedestal's trapezoidal top face position.

For the pump body, it looks like it's stored rotated, with a long cylindrical shape, two flange strips (roughly 180 units long) at opposite ends, and a bulging middle section where the spout attaches. I'm trying to pin down the direction and dimensions of these flange strips to reconstruct the body's true orientation.

I'm tracing the body's outline between the two flanges, checking the edge coordinates on each side to estimate the column width (roughly 115 units) as it runs from near flange A toward flange B.

Tracing further, the taper continues from width 115 down near the shoulder, then there's an end face around 118 long marking a transition, followed by a bulge section that connects into the outer strip running toward the B flange — so the shape seems to step: narrow column, shoulder, bulge, then B flange.

Thinking about a real hand pump structure, this likely corresponds to base flange, cylinder body, air chamber bulge, and top flange where the cap sits, with the spout mounted at the bulge's widest point. So A is probably the bottom flange and B the top, meaning I need to orient the axis from A to B pointing upward and rotate the whole geometry accordingly.

I'm setting up a local coordinate frame along the body's axis to measure the bulge width relative to the flange widths and confirm proportions make sense.

Continuing to trace flange B's thickness and bulge, I find its outer/inner faces give thickness around 21 with v ranging roughly −20 to 164. Checking points further along the bulge on both sides, the lower side reaches v near 149 while the upper side approaches a symmetric negative value.

Pulling this together, the body seems to run from flange A at the bottom through a column, into the bulge, then flange B at top — matching the "upper bulge" description. I'm now working out the rotation needed to align the body's axis vertically on screen, computing the angle from the axis vector components.

With that rotation determined, the orientation seems fine since the body is roughly symmetric, so flip ambiguity shouldn't matter much. I'm now puzzling over the spout's placement — its flange face is described as the right edge, attaching at the body's widest bulge point, which tells me which direction the spout extends from there.

Refining the axis angle by using the flange strip's endpoints, I compute the direction vector and get about 110.1°, so the rotation needed is roughly −110°, which I'll use going forward to transform points from local body coordinates into the final frame.

Checking the transformation against the known u and v direction vectors confirms it's mapping correctly: x' corresponds to v, and y' corresponds to −u. Using this, I set the centerline at v≈73.5 giving x'=73.5, and I'm working out the bottom flange's underside position using u≈65.

Now I'm pinning down the flange B top face at u≈405, giving a total height of 340, and locating the widest point of the bulge around u≈312-315 by comparing v-values at different u positions along the upper and lower edges. I'm also trying to find the left edge of the bulge where v is minimized, checking several candidate points near u≈287-345 to pin down exactly where the spout attaches.

Working through the coordinate transforms, I find the minimum v value reaches about -6.7 at a u-coordinate near 326, which marks the narrowest point along that side of the bulge outline.

Now I need to work out the cap geometry: its skirt underside rests on the top flange face, with the link bar's lower eye connecting to a lug on the cap's upper surface. I'm tracing the cap's outline—a skirt base plus dome shape, with a lug on top containing two holes for the link bar attachment.

I'm tracing the two long edges of the cap outline, measuring their directions and lengths to figure out whether they form the dome side versus the skirt side of the shape.

Setting up a coordinate transform along and perpendicular to line1's direction to measure where the skirt underside sits relative to the rest of the outline — computing projected values for each point to see how far the skirt spans and where other features line up relative to it.

That cap range from -40 to 111 doesn't fit a skirt-at-edge arrangement, so I need to reconsider — maybe that first line is actually the boundary of the dome shape itself, with the filled polygon tracing out the dome's outline through a series of coordinate points.

Continuing those coordinate calculations, I'm finding the strip spans roughly t from -35 to -3.5 with a width around 141, which looks like it could be the skirt's underside along the outer long edge. There's then a gap between this strip and the dome region where other decorative features like a lug sit.

Checking the lug circles, both pairs land at the same w value of 259.6, suggesting they're aligned along t and positioned beyond the dome's w range—this makes me reconsider whether the cap's actual vertical axis runs along w rather than t, which would change my whole orientation assumption for the upright position.

Actually, since the two holes differ only in t (by 49), that spacing must represent the vertical direction, meaning t is the up axis after all, with the skirt underside sitting at the bottom near t=-35.

But now the dome and lug extents don't line up with the skirt's w range, which makes me question that assumption — maybe the real "up" axis is actually w instead, and I'm looking at this as a side profile where the cap body's long axis runs along w.

Working through more of the t-values along the outline, I see t peaks around 121 near w≈100-150 before tapering off at the extremes. Overall this traces a large dome-shaped outer boundary spanning t from about -40 to 121 and w from 26 to 283.

This looks like a dome with a flat skirt and possibly a lug feature at one end, drawn with layered dark outline strokes and lighter inner fills. I'm trying to figure out orientation -- whether the curved dome faces up or the flat skirt does, and whether the lug end has holes through it.

I'm reasoning through which axis is "up" for the cap by checking whether two holes sit side by side or stacked, which would tell me if the lug extends sideways or vertically relative to the skirt.

The naming is ambiguous enough that I need to work out the geometry from the actual coordinates rather than trust the labels.

I'm tracing through the (t,w) pairs along the outline to measure the shape's width at each height, trying to see if the profile narrows like a dome near the top or stays wide, which should tell me which end is really the cap and which is the skirt.

Continuing to compute the time and distance weight deltas across more coordinate pairs, tracking how these values shift as the points progress along the path.

Still computing coordinate differences...

Continuing to compute the time and weight values along this trajectory as the points converge toward the end of the path.

Mapping out the remaining width/thickness pairs, I'm seeing the overall shape emerge: a narrow lug region on the left (w 26-60), then a large dome-shaped lobe spanning w 60-210 with a flat bottom strip and a peak thickness around 122, followed by another lug region on the right side (w 211-283).

I'm testing different orientation hypotheses for "up" (whether it corresponds to t, -t, w, or -w) to figure out whether this cross-section represents a hemispherical dome with ear-like mounting lugs on each side, since the two hole circles stack vertically in the right lobe.

Looking more carefully, I'm measuring the skirt's width and comparing it to the body width at different heights — the body actually seems wider than the skirt below it, which is throwing off my earlier dome assumption.

Thinking through the hand pump mechanism: the link bar connects the cap's lug to the handle's fulcrum hole, the handle's end hole links to the piston rod's top eye, and the rod runs down through the cap into the body, while the handle's far end serves as the grip. That suggests the lug sits off to one side of the cap with the link rising vertically to the fulcrum, putting the handle's piston-side hole above the body center and the lug offset to the right.

I'm working out the coordinate transform to confirm which way "right" points by checking the rotation that maps the t-axis to straight up, which tells me the w-axis maps to positive x -- so the lug should be positioned to the right.

Now I'm applying that same rotation to the skirt and corner points, converting their (w,t) coordinates into the upright (X,Y) frame to see where the bottom edge and corners land.

I'll assume the cap's central axis aligns with the body's centerline, with a small ear feature on the left side. Now I'm working out the link bar geometry, locating the hole centers from the circle endpoints given in the data.

Finding the two hole centers gives roughly (27.97,27.81) and (30.26,184.78), about 157 units apart, mostly vertical with a slight horizontal offset — so I'm computing the bar's rotation from that top-to-bottom vector.

The link's orientation actually depends on the lug and handle positions, so I need to work out the handle geometry next. Looking at the handle lever's stored coordinates, I'm extracting its hole centers from the circle corner points—finding the big hole at roughly (30.07, 30.09) and locating a second, smaller hole further along the shape.

I'm also calculating a third, small middle hole center around (173.34, 130.2) and figuring out the handle's path and curvature from the left end through this middle hole toward the far grip end near (470, 470), estimating the direction angles along each segment.

Now I'm thinking through the handle's working orientation — which end attaches to the piston rod, which is the pivot, and which is the grip — so I can determine the correct rotation to apply to the stored shape, with the left hole starting near (30,30).

With the horizontal span fixed at 123 and handle length 174.8, the vertical offset works out to about 124.2 — but there's still ambiguity about whether M sits above or below E. I need to reason about which orientation actually matches a working pump handle, with the link bar connecting up from the lug to the handle's middle hole.

Testing two options: in one, the handle slopes down to the right, putting E well above M and the lug, which would put the rod top around 281 above L; in the other, the handle slopes up to the right, putting E only about 33 above L — closer to the cap's dome level. I need to check which placement makes physical sense given where the piston rod and cap sit.

Comparing the dome top (97 above the lug hole) to E at 33 above the lug rules out option B, since that would put E inside the dome. So option A holds — the handle tilts downward toward the grip end, matching the stored orientation's modest rotation. Working out the required vector from E to M (123 horizontal, 124 vertical) gives an angle of about 45.3°, versus the stored handle angle of about 35°, meaning roughly a 10° clockwise rotation is needed, though the link's tilt isn't necessarily perfectly vertical so there's some flexibility there.

Now I'm turning to the rod to pin down the geometry more precisely — computing the rod's top eye hole center from its four corner points (roughly 315.8, 25.4 with radius 5.77) and tracing its direction down toward the bottom end to constrain the handle's rotation further.

I'm tracing the rod's axis mathematically, computing the direction vector from the eye center and projecting along it to locate where the strip's edges converge toward the piston end structure.

That confirms the axis direction at roughly 160°, so I'm projecting both end points onto that axis to check they give the same distance from the eye, confirming the rod length is consistent at around 322 units.

Rotating the rod by −70° so the eye sits at top and tip at bottom, keeping it vertical through the body. I'm now checking how the cap height and flange position constrain where the eye lands relative to the piston hole.

With the link vertical, computing L.y and E.y from the cap geometry puts the rod tip above the flange face rather than inside the bore—so the eye position must be lower than I first assumed. I need to adjust E.y so the tip actually falls inside the body, treating "inside the body" as a looser tolerance on the y-range rather than an exact point.

That puts the tip too deep, overlapping into the cap dome region, which doesn't look physically sound either. I'm second-guessing the cap height and lug placement assumptions, trying to reconcile body height, rod length, and link length so the tip lands somewhere inside the body during the stroke rather than colliding with the cap.

Now I'm working out the link-bar geometry algebraically: expressing the handle pivot point as a function of the lug position plus the link vector, then relating that to the eye position through the handle's fixed length and angle, so I can solve for the angle that keeps the tip position consistent with the body depth.

Testing φ=35° gives a=20.2, b=155.7, which places the tip right at the top of the bore — close to the flange face but a bit too shallow for comfort.

But I realize the random-rotation assumption undermines this: if each part is stored at an arbitrary angle, I can't rely on nice numbers like 7.4° tilt matching anything meaningful. Without that constraint, I need another way to pin down the actual orientation.

So maybe pulled-down grip equals rod-up, fine either way. The real handle orientation needs to be within 8° of my estimate, so φ is the free parameter I need to pin down given the link length and pivot constraints — if the link is vertical, I get φ around 45.3°, which is close to my working value.

Testing other link tilts: at a=20 I get φ≈35°, and within the 8° tolerance a φ near 40° gives a tip position just below the flange face, while φ=45° pushes it noticeably above, and φ=30° shifts things again. None of these cleanly land the tip right at the flange, so I'm trying to narrow down which tilt gives the most consistent result.

I'm now wondering if the cap lug's assumed position is off rather than the angle — maybe the true design has the rod tip deeper inside the body than I'm computing, which would mean the handle's stored angle and link tilt are different from my guesses. Since the exact geometry is uncertain, I'll settle on something in the 30-35° range that puts the tip modestly inside the body, treating that as close enough given the tolerance.

I'll pick an angle of 34.95° with zero additional rotation, since the handle's stored rotation is arbitrary anyway and might just land there by coincidence. Now I need to work out the world coordinates — placing the base plate via translation, keeping it unrotated, and locating the pedestal's top face, which sits somewhere around y=5 to 8.3 based on the outline strokes.

Looking at the outer and inner paths, the visual top face is roughly y=5.5-6, and the pedestal spans x from about 80.5 to 210.4, centering around 145.4 — close to the base plate's own center of 145.5, which spans x=5 to 286 with its bottom edge at y=88. Now I'm stacking up the total height on a 1376x768 canvas: body height of 340 plus the cap section above the flange, accounting for the rod eye positioned well above that.

Tracing the handle and rod geometry upward from the base, the topmost point (handle top) ends up roughly 25 units above its anchor point E, which itself sits 340+318 units above the pedestal top — pushing the total height uncomfortably close to 772, just over the 768 canvas limit, so I need to double-check these offsets carefully.

The grip end stays safely within bounds at Ybase+455's equivalent, so that's not the constraint; I'm now checking whether φ=45 gives more breathing room.

This confirms the layout is scaled to just fit the canvas height with minimal margin, so I should pick Ybase around 686 and work out the other placements accordingly, starting with the base plate pedestal's x and y translation values.

Measuring flange thickness on both faces gives differing results (16.3 vs 21.8), which is a bit inconsistent but workable, and I'm now setting up to compute the body's rotation transform assuming exactly −110° to align the axis upward.

Settling on w_c=136 as the dome centerline, I'm working out the world-space translation: cx=464 to align with x=600, and cy=305.5 derived from the skirt underside position, confirming the rotation math checks out.

Computing the lug upper hole position gives world coordinates (723.7, 279.6), sitting 123.7 off the centerline, which looks sensible given the spout is on the left and the handle/grip extend rightward. Now I'm working through the rod eye and link geometry, placing the lower eye and computing the upper eye position via the handle's local offsets, then setting up to solve for the link length b from the horizontal gap between the two eyes.

I find the handle's top edge lands just slightly off-canvas by about 1.4 units, so I'm considering small adjustments—shifting the whole layout down a couple pixels or tweaking the handle rotation angle—to bring everything back within bounds.

Now I need to set up the transform for the handle: translate to E's position, rotate −2°, then translate back from its local origin, verifying M maps correctly. Finally placing the rod's transform using the eye center as the pivot point.

Tracing out the spout's outline coordinates, I'm finding a thin rounded strip running from around (80,66) to (136,11) that looks like the nozzle's end-lip detail.

Working out which edge of the bar is the outer flange face versus the mating face, comparing the two parallel edges' coordinates against the tube's position to figure out the correct polygon points for the flange fill shape.

Continuing the rotation math, I find the outer bulge lands slightly left and up relative to center, while the mouth point shifts further left and down—confirming the spout curves outward then down as expected.

More transformed points confirm the spout curves downward with the inner edge checking out consistently, and no mirroring issues—just a pure rotation. I'm now checking whether the tube's bulge sits correctly on the convex top side by transforming the flange-end corner coordinates.

Checking the spout's downward curve and its clearance beneath the attach point, the cap's dome orientation at −55° rotation, and the handle grip position on the right side — all seem consistent and non-conflicting.
